title: Go to Bed
dateline: Selrick Academy. The first weeks as partners.
mood: Plans in three colors of ink, a phone call at two in the morning, and a front held alone for two minutes.

hero.alt: One of Guinevere's drones up close: a round gray shell with cat ears, a yellow ring glowing in each ear, two yellow eyes, and a red fist floating beside it above the city.

segs.t: The first plan came under Vexana’s door before the bells. It was written in three colors of ink.
Guinevere’s lines were pink.
Run, twice round the grounds. Bag, two hundred, left hand only (medic).
Vexana’s lines were violet.
Run, the same. Forms, fifty.
At the bottom, in gold:
Rest, five minutes. If earned.
Under that was a phone number, underlined twice.
For emergencies. Or anything.
They ran at first light. Guinevere’s right arm was still bound from shoulder to elbow. It did nothing to slow her mouth.
She talked for the whole run, twenty minutes. Drone angles. Every pair in the year, and which of them she could beat.
Vexana said two words. One was “Yes.” The other was “Left,” when Guinevere, still talking, nearly ran into the fountain.
In the training hall Vexana did her forms down on the floor now, under the high windows.
At the fiftieth form she stopped and lowered her practice staff.
Guinevere looked over from the bag. “You can do more than fifty, you know.”
“It says fifty.”
She sat on the bench by the door and watched the hall clock for five minutes exactly. Then she stood up.
Guinevere stared at her. “You did all of it.”
“It was the plan.”
“Nobody does all of it! I write extra so I’ll at least do half.”
“Then write what you mean.”
Guinevere beamed. Then she stopped beaming. She read her own pink line again,
two hundred
, and went back to the bag.
At two in the morning Vexana looked up from her desk. Across the grounds, through her window, the training hall was still lit.
Another hour and her drones will sag,
she thought. She had watched them sag from the gallery for a year.
She took out the plan and dialed the number in gold.
It rang a long time.
“I’m asleep,” said Guinevere’s voice. She was out of breath. Behind her the hall’s high roof threw the words back.
“Go to bed,” said Vexana.
A pause. “Vexana? What’s wrong?”
“Nothing.”
“Then what’s the emergency?”
“Go to bed.”
Vexana put the phone down. Across the grounds the lights burned for one more minute. Then the hall went dark, and Vexana went to bed too.
At the run the next morning, Guinevere fell in beside her. “You phoned me at two in the morning to tell me to go to bed.”
“Yes.”
“That number was for emergencies!”
“It was one.”
Guinevere opened her mouth and shut it again. “Fine,” she said at last. “Fair.”
After that, whenever the hall stayed lit late, Vexana phoned. Guinevere stopped saying she was asleep. She bargained.
“Ten more.”
“Go to bed.”
“Five. You can count them.”
Down the line the bag thudded, slow and hard. Vexana counted.
“That was six,” she said.
“The last one was for you.”
One afternoon a drone of Guinevere’s came back from drills with a dent in its shell. It flew crooked and kept sinking.
“It won’t hold its height,” said Guinevere. “I told it twice. After everything I’ve done for that drone!”
They sat on the grass at the edge of the training field. Vexana’s cloth bag lay at her feet. She held out her hand.
Guinevere sent the drone to her. Vexana opened the shell on her knee with a thumbnail. Under the left ear, a bracket was bent. She set two fingers on it and pressed until it was straight.
“A bracket,” she said. “It was bent.”
“You can do that?”
“Yes.”
Guinevere looked at the cloth bag. “You carry that bag everywhere. What’s in it?”
“Tools.”
Guinevere leaned closer. “Who taught you? Your family?”
Vexana’s fingers stopped on the shell. For a breath she saw smoke, and her father’s back.
“I don’t talk about that.”
“Then I won’t ask,” said Guinevere. “Not ever.”
She lay back on the grass, hands behind her head, and squinted at the sun. “I’m not afraid of the dark.”
She says that lying in the sun,
thought Vexana.
Let her stay there.
She clicked the shell shut. The drone rose off her knee, ears up, and held its height.
The night of the fish-market raid.
Under Vexana’s lamp the fish-market drone still lay open, one ear bent flat. Her phone lay face down beside it.
The bracket was half straight under the same two fingers. Her hand had stopped shaking.
The first weeks as partners. The day of the team test.
That morning’s plan had one line, in gold.
Team test. Win it. (I mean it.)

Six rails ran the length of the training field to a chalk square, with the steel dummies from the trial waiting on them. Today a pair stood in the square, and every rail ran at once. A pair was out the moment a steel arm touched either of them.
Guinevere’s right arm was out of its binding now, the skin along it new and pink. She rolled her shoulder and took the front of the square.
Over her shoulder she saw Vexana set her cloth bag down in the corner and raise her staff.
The bell rang.
The first waves were easy. Guinevere met each dummy as its chest opened, with a fist or a drone. Vexana’s bolts went over her shoulder into whatever she missed.
In the fourth minute two dummies came down the outside rails together. Guinevere took the right. The left one swung for her back.
Behind her, steel rang on the staff. Something cracked. Guinevere sent a drone back blind, and it knocked the dummy up its rail.
Then the bolts stopped.
She glanced back. Vexana was down on one knee. A split ran up the grip of her staff, just below the orb, and the orb had gone dark.
“Hold the front,” said Vexana. She was already pulling the old toolbox out of her bag.
“How long?”
“Two minutes.”
Six rails,
thought Guinevere.
Fine.
She stepped to the middle of the front, raised both fists and shouted at the top of her voice.
“I am the herald of dawn, and the one who lights starlight in the dark of night.”
The dummies came.
She went left, then right, then left again. A steel arm passed a hand from her ear. Her new skin pulled at every punch. Her drones flew lower with every pass. She did not let them drop.
Nothing got past her into the square.
Between two blows she looked back, once.

Vexana knelt on the grass beside the old toolbox she carried everywhere, its lid open. She was fitting a brass collar over the split. In her fingers a small screwdriver with a worn grip went round a quarter turn at a time. Her hands did not hurry.
She isn’t even looking up,
thought Guinevere.
She knows I’ll hold.
She turned back just in time to duck.
Violet light spilled past her onto the grass. Behind her, Vexana’s voice rang out.
“Awaken the dawn!”
Bolts went past both of Guinevere’s ears. Above her something hummed. She did not turn around. The last three rails went still.
The bell rang. Every dummy hung dead on its rail, and both of them were on their feet.
Guinevere turned around, out of breath and grinning. “You said two minutes.”
“It took less,” said Vexana.
That night the training hall was dark. Vexana phoned anyway.
“Go to bed.”
“Yes, yes.” Guinevere yawned into the phone. “Vexana. At the test, when you were down there, you didn’t even...”
The sentence never finished. After a while came a small snore.
Vexana kept the phone at her ear.
From her knees she had looked up once. There had been nothing but Guinevere’s back, and steel coming at it.
She’s standing where my father stood,
she had thought. Her hands had wanted to shake. She had made herself look down at the screwdriver, a quarter turn at a time.
At the bell the back had turned around, and there was Guinevere’s grin.
She ended the call and set the phone down. It stayed quiet.
Her staff lay across her lap. The collar was a spare from her father’s toolbox, kept for the gun sights on the city wall. Now it held the cracked grip together.
Her thumb went round the brass once and stayed there.
